articles.title: An Australian billionaire couple donates $120 million to 10 conservation groups to protect wildlife; one rare parrot with fewer than 180 left could be saved
articles.summary: An Australian billionaire couple has committed more than $120 million to 10 conservation organisations in one of the country's largest philanthropic
articles.body: An Australian billionaire couple has committed more than $120 million to 10 conservation organisations in one of the country's largest philanthropic contributions towards environmental protection. Alexandra and Julian Burt, through their Wright Burt Foundation, are supporting initiatives focused on protecting threatened wildlife, restoring natural habitats and expanding conservation efforts across Australia. Among the beneficiaries is BirdLife Australia, which will receive $10 million to support the recovery of the critically endangered Western Ground Parrot, also known as Kyloring. Fewer than 180 of these birds are believed to remain in the wild. The wider commitment will also fund land acquisition, ecosystem restoration and scientific research, including efforts to expand protected habitats and strengthen the recovery of threatened native species.Who are Alexandra and Julian Burt?Alexandra and Julian Burt are Australian philanthropists who have committed the funding through their charitable organisation, the Wright Burt Foundation.Alexandra is the granddaughter of mining entrepreneur Peter Wright, who was a business partner of Lang Hancock, the father of Australian mining billionaire Gina Rinehart. The Wright and Hancock families were associated with the development of Western Australia's iron ore industry.The couple generally maintain a low public profile and support several causes through their foundation, including environmental protection, education, arts and heritage.Julian Burt has spoken about his longstanding interest in nature, recalling how he kept ant farms, raised pigeons and even kept redback spiders in jars during his childhood.The couple also owns Bullo River Station, a cattle property in Australia's Northern Territory. The property is managed in partnership with the Australian Wildlife Conservancy, combining cattle-station operations with conservation and wildlife-protection initiatives.How will the $120 million be distributed?The Wright Burt Foundation's commitment will be shared among 10 Australian environmental and conservation organisations. Three organisations will receive $25 million each, two will receive $10 million each, while the remaining five will receive approximately $5.33 million apiece.The reported allocations are:Australian Wildlife Conservancy: $25 millionBush Heritage Australia: $25 millionGreenpeace: $25 millionBirdLife Australia: $10 millionGreat Southern Land Conservancy: $10 millionAussie Ark: approximately $5.33 millionConservation Partners: approximately $5.33 millionGreat Barrier Reef Foundation: approximately $5.33 millionRainforest Rescue: approximately $5.33 millionSouth Endeavour Trust: approximately $5.33 millionThe individual figures are rounded, so their combined total differs slightly from the reported commitment of more than $120 million.The contributions will support different aspects of conservation, including wildlife recovery, habitat restoration, land acquisition, environmental research and ecosystem protection.$10 million donation could help save Australia's rare parrotOne of the most significant projects supported by the donation is the recovery of the Western Ground Parrot, also known by its Noongar name, Kyloring.BirdLife Australia will receive $10 million to accelerate efforts to prevent the species from becoming extinct. The bird is classified as Critically Endangered, with fewer than 180 individuals believed to remain in the wild.The majority of the remaining population, approximately 150 birds, is found in Cape Arid National Park on Western Australia's south coast. A smaller population survives in the Waychinicup-Manypeaks area, while birds are also part of a captive conservation programme at Perth Zoo.The species faces several threats, including extensive bushfires, habitat degradation and predation by invasive animals such as feral cats and foxes.BirdLife Australia said experts had previously estimated a 75% likelihood that the Western Ground Parrot would become extinct by 2038 without urgent intervention. This is a risk estimate rather than a confirmed extinction timeline.The new funding will support a recovery programme involving the movement of birds between wild populations, habitat protection, improved monitoring and efforts to increase breeding success.Researchers also plan to improve methods for locating and monitoring nests, while strengthening fire management and invasive-predator control in important habitats.The programme will involve collaboration with Western Australia's Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions and Noongar Traditional Custodians.Australian Wildlife Conservancy receives $25 millionThe Australian Wildlife Conservancy (AWC) will receive $25 million to expand its conservation operations and protect threatened native species.The organisation currently manages conservation programmes across approximately 1.7% of Australia's landmass. It aims to expand this to 5%, an area comparable in size to Germany.The funding will support strategic land acquisitions, the establishment and management of wildlife sanctuaries, habitat restoration and efforts to control invasive predators, particularly feral cats.It will also allow the organisation to expand scientific research into lesser-studied wildlife. One initiative will focus on bats, which account for more than 20% of mammal species but are often overlooked in conservation programmes.AWC plans to survey its sanctuaries to identify bat populations, determine which species are threatened and improve scientific understanding of their distribution.The organisation has also been working with the Burts at Bullo River Station, combining cattle-station management with scientific conservation and habitat restoration.Bush Heritage Australia plans to acquire a 20,333-hectare propertyBush Heritage Australia will also receive $25 million, with part of the funding expected to support the proposed acquisition of Wooroora Station, a cattle property covering approximately 20,333 hectares, around 100 kilometres south-west of Cairns in Queensland.The property contains rainforest, woodland and other important habitats. It provides habitat for several native species, including southern cassowaries, koalas, yellow-bellied gliders and Lumholtz's tree-kangaroos.Approximately 98% of its natural landscape remains intact, making it an important area for biodiversity protection.The property is located near Bush Heritage Australia's existing Yourka Reserve. Protecting the two landscapes could help create a larger connected habitat for wildlife.The organisation has described the proposed acquisition as an important conservation opportunity. The property should not yet be described as a completed purchase or an established conservation reserve.Other organisations receiving fundingThe remaining contributions will support several other environmental initiatives across Australia.Greenpeace will receive $25 million. The organisation works on environmental issues including climate change, forest protection and ocean conservation. However, a detailed breakdown of how this particular grant will be allocated has not been publicly established.Great Southern Land Conservancy will receive $10 million to support land acquisition and conservation management.Aussie Ark will receive approximately $5.33 million to accelerate its three-year conservation masterplan. The organisation's work includes breeding, habitat restoration and rewilding programmes involving threatened native species such as Tasmanian devils, eastern quolls and Manning River turtles.Rainforest Rescue will also receive approximately $5.33 million. Much of the funding will support its Daintree Oxbow Project, which aims to protect and restore approximately 600 hectares of ecologically important land in Queensland. The remaining money will strengthen the organisation's capacity to undertake long-term restoration work.The Great Barrier Reef Foundation, Conservation Partners and South Endeavour Trust are also among the beneficiaries. The specific project-level allocation of their respective grants has not been established in the public announcements reviewed.Australia faces growing biodiversity challengesThe donation comes as Australia's native wildlife faces increasing pressure from habitat loss, invasive species, climate change and extreme weather events.According to Australia's Environment Report 2025, the country's threatened-species list reached 2,175, following the addition of 39 species during the year. The report also identified climate change as a threat affecting nine out of 10 newly listed species.The funding is expected to provide conservation organisations with additional resources to pursue long-term projects, acquire ecologically important habitats and strengthen programmes aimed at preventing further wildlife declines.For the Western Ground Parrot, the $10 million contribution to BirdLife Australia provides additional support for an urgent recovery programme. For other conservation organisations, the wider commitment could help expand protected landscapes, restore ecosystems and support threatened species across Australia.You use AI every day. articles.title: A retired Navy SEAL commander removed a hemlock on a New Hampshire lakefront boundary, prompting two felony charges; both were dropped, and he paid a $1,000 fine despite an $11,259 appraisal of the trees
articles.summary: A retired US Navy SEAL commander who faced two felony charges for removing a tree along a shared property boundary in New Hampshire has paid a $1,000 fine
articles.body: A retired US Navy SEAL commander who faced two felony charges for removing a tree along a shared property boundary in New Hampshire has paid a $1,000 fine after both charges were dropped. Michael Hayes, 55, pleaded guilty to a non-criminal trespassing violation in a court hearing on October 23.According to AOL.com, the case began after Hayes removed a hemlock tree standing along the boundary between his lakefront property and a neighbouring property owned by Stacey Nath-Vinick and Michael Vinick. The neighbours had valued the removed tree and a nearby stump at $11,259, according to a report by the Valley News.A Sullivan County grand jury indicted Hayes on May 27 on charges of criminal mischief and timber-harvesting trespass. Both offences carried possible prison sentences of up to seven years. However, prosecutors agreed to drop the two felony charges during the October hearing.Hayes accepted a lesser trespassing violation and paid the $1,000 fine at the court clerk's office before leaving. Judge James Kennedy presided over the hearing at Sullivan Superior Court in Newport. Hayes was represented by attorney Jason Casey of Hinckley Allen.Why Hayes removed the boundary treeThe hemlock stood on the shared boundary between Hayes's lakefront property and the neighbouring lot to the south. The Vinicks own the adjoining property.Hayes said he feared the tree was dead or dying during the summer of 2025. He also pointed to an earlier incident in 2017, when a falling tree destroyed a family vehicle. A letter from Mercedes-Benz documenting the incident was obtained by the Valley News.On June 11,Hayes emailed the Vinicks to ask whether the hemlock could be removed. This was a day after Michael Vinick's father died. Nath-Vinick later told the court that she responded by saying the family was dealing with a death.The tree was removed a few days later. A four-foot stump from another hemlock, which the Vinicks had cut in 2019, was also removed. Hayes had claimed that the neighbours cut the earlier tree without his permission.According to court filings described by the Valley News, an arborist hired by Hayes for a drainage project had told him that the hemlock was dying. The tree was also leaning towards the neighbours' house and was likely to fall soon.The Town of Sunapee's tree-cutting request form lists the removal and replacement of decaying trees and shrubs among activities that do not require a permit.Neighbours valued the trees at $11,259About a month after the tree was removed, the Vinicks hired arboricultural consultant Brian Beaty to assess the damage. Beaty was registered with the American Society of Consulting Arborists and the International Society of Arboriculture.He rated the hemlock's condition at 53% on a scale ranging from 10% to 100%. His assessment placed the replacement value of the removed tree and the neighbouring stump at $11,259.Beaty also noted that the stump had supported a hammock regularly used by Michael Vinick.After the grand jury indicted Hayes, he hired Jeffrey Coombs, president of Ossipee Mountain Land Company, a forest management and firewood business. Coombs examined photographs of the trees and gave a different assessment.He described two remaining hemlocks along the boundary as being in "an advanced state of decline". He also said they had "no positive market value".The difference between the two assessments became an important part of Hayes's defence. His lawyer argued that Beaty's report calculated the cost of replacing the tree rather than its market value.In a July memo to County Attorney Christine Hilliard, Casey said this difference weakened the state's claim about the financial loss caused by the removal. He also argued that Hayes had not acted recklessly and described the incident as "a good-faith misunderstanding regarding authorisation".What the two felony charges involvedThe charges against Hayes were based on two New Hampshire laws concerning damage to property and unauthorised tree removal.Under state law RSA 227-J:8-a, cutting or destroying trees on land belonging to another person without permission can amount to a criminal offence if the action is reckless. The offence becomes a class B felony when the market-value loss exceeds $1,000. A lower loss can result in a misdemeanour charge.The second charge, criminal mischief under RSA 634:2, applies when a person purposely causes or attempts to cause financial loss. It becomes a felony when the loss exceeds $1,500.The state would have had to establish the required financial loss and intent or recklessness to secure felony convictions under the respective laws.New Hampshire also has a separate civil provision for cases involving trees cut without permission. Under RSA 227-J:8, a person who negligently cuts a tree on someone else's property may have to pay between three and 10 times the tree's market value to the affected owner.The Valley News did not report whether the Vinicks had filed a separate civil claim.Hayes told the Valley News that he accepted responsibility for a violation rather than a criminal offence because he wanted the matter to end as quickly as possible.In June, he had also said that he was not contacted before the charges were filed. He described this as "most regrettable and concerning".You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'This is not UCC, but Hindu Civil Code': Owaisi targets Maharashtra govt, says move seeks to 'snatch' Muslims' identity
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: AIMIM president Asaduddin Owaisi on Tuesday slammed the Maharashtra government's proposed Uniform Civil Code (UCC), alleging that it was aimed
articles.body: NEW DELHI: AIMIM president Asaduddin Owaisi on Tuesday slammed the Maharashtra government's proposed Uniform Civil Code (UCC), alleging that it was aimed at targeting Muslims and imposing a "Hindu Civil Code" on non-Hindu communities.Questioning the government's approach, Owaisi asked, "Why accept tribal customs but not Muslim practices?" He alleged that the proposed code would restrict Muslims from following their religious practices, particularly those related to marriage and divorce."This UCC is being brought to stop Muslims from practising their religion. In Islam, marriage is a contract. You are also imposing divorce rules as per the Hindu Marriage Act. All this is being done to target Muslims and snatch their identity," he said, ANI reported.Owaisi said Nikah was an essential part of marriage under Islam and argued that different religions followed distinct personal laws adding that, "In Islam, marriage is called nikah. It is not a religious ritual. Nikah is a contract, not a lifelong bond."If there is no nikah, then what is it? If a child is born out of a relationship, does that make it a marriage? No, it is not a marriage, he said.He also argued that the UCC would give legal rights to children born out of live-in relationships, which he said was not permitted under Islamic religious practices.Owaisi made the remarks at a press conference after the Mahayuti government invited public suggestions on implementing the UCC in Maharashtra and released a questionnaire for the consultation.He claimed the questionnaire indicated that the Devendra Fadnavis-led government had already decided to implement the code."The subject of the press conference today is that the Maharashtra Government has invited opinions from the public to implement UCC. The state government has also prepared a questionnaire for it. This questionnaire, prepared by the Maharashtra government, makes it clear that the Devendra Fadnavis govt will implement the UCC," he said.Owaisi questioned the questionnaire's focus on polygamy and extra-judicial divorce, alleging that it did not address the Hindu Undivided Family (HUF)."The questionnaire consists of leading questions on polygamy and extra-judicial divorce. But there is not one question on Hindu Undivided Family," he said.He compared the proposed exercise with UCC initiatives undertaken by BJP governments in Gujarat, Uttarakhand, Assam and Madhya Pradesh, claiming that these were attempts to impose a "Hindu Civil Code" on non-Hindu communities."This makes it evident that, much like the initiatives introduced by BJP governments in Gujarat, Uttarakhand, Assam, and Madhya Pradesh under the guise of a 'Uniform Civil Code,' this is not a true UCC, but rather a 'Hindu Civil Code' that is being imposed upon non-Hindu communities," Owaisi said.He also objected to the format of the questionnaire, saying most of its questions were framed to elicit yes-or-no responses."Additionally, if you examine the questionnaire, you will find that the majority of the questions are framed in a 'yes or no' format," he added.Owaisi also linked the resignation of retired Bombay High court judge RC Chavan to the composition of the exercise. He said Chavan had cited the absence of a member from the minority community as a reason for stepping down."I believe this is precisely why RC Chavan, a retired judge of the Bombay HC, chose to resign. He had stated that there is no one from the minority community," he said."They are talking about implementation in the state of Maharashtra at this juncture, but they are not defining what this 'uniform' actually is," he added.Meanwhile, Maharashtra Chief minister Devendra Fadnavis defended his government's decision to draft a UCC, saying the Constitution directs states to work towards its implementation. Hitting back at Owaisi, Fadnavis said the UCC was rooted in the Directive Principles of State Policy.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India on Tuesday strongly criticised the United States Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF) over its remarks on the alleged
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India on Tuesday strongly criticised the United States Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF) over its remarks on the alleged targeting of religious places, including Gurudwaras, churches and mosques, in the country.Responding to a question from ANI, ministry of external affairs (MEA) spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal described the USCIRF as a “biased and ill-informed organisation” with a “blatantly political agenda”.He also accused the US-based body and its commissioners of remaining silent on attacks on religious places in the United States, as well as hate crimes and racial abuse targeting the Indian community there.“It is particularly telling, and you must note that the USCIRF and its commissioners have consistently kept silent on attacks on religious places in the United States, as well as on hate crimes and racial abuse that are targeted at the Indian community in the United States,” Jaiswal said.“Prejudiced entities like the USCIRF can hardly be taken seriously,” he added.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Deal to create world's biggest electricity company, worth $67 billion, is in trouble; residents fear it will...
articles.summary: A $67 billion deal that would create the world's largest retail electricity company is running into fierce resistance in Virginia.
articles.body: A $67 billion deal that would create the world's largest retail electricity company is running into fierce resistance in Virginia. Florida-based NextEra Energy wants to buy Richmond-headquartered Dominion Energy, but the state's governor, its attorney general and a growing number of residents say the merger offers Virginians too little and could push their power bills even higher.The fight comes as electricity prices climb across the US, driven partly by the power demand of AI data centres. Virginia is where that boom is most visible. Dominion, which has 3.6 million customers across three states, serves Northern Virginia's Data Center Alley, the world's largest cluster of such facilities. The State Corporation Commission (SCC), which must approve the deal, is set to rule in January, and needs two of its three commissioners on board.Virginia wants a rate freeze, NextEra is saying noGovernor Abigail Spanberger, a Democrat, wants electricity rates frozen for six years and bill credits of $29 a month for four years for current Dominion customers. "My priority is affordability for Virginians," she told reporters ahead of a public hearing last week, The New York Times reported.NextEra's offer is much smaller: $10 a month in credits for four years, plus $100 million for bill assistance to lower-income households and workforce programmes. In a filing this week, chief executive John Ketchum rejected the freeze, saying it should be handled in routine rate-setting cases rather than the merger review.The companies have tried to narrow the gap. Earlier this month, they accepted 101 of 117 conditions proposed by the SCC staff and the state's consumer counsel, including two independent directors on the Virginia utility's board and up to $5 billion in spending with local businesses over five years. They still refused the freeze and a staff proposal for a three-year rate cap.Wall Street has noticed the standoff. The premium on NextEra's all-stock offer has shrunk from 23% in May to under 2%.Virginians are paying over 10% more for electricity than a year agoUS Energy Information Administration figures cited by the NYT show Virginians paid an average of $176 a month in August for 1,000 kilowatt-hours of electricity, up from $159 a year earlier. The national average rose from $176 to $182.That strain was on display outside the SCC hearing in Richmond, where dozens of protesters, several of them local pastors, held signs reading "Take Back Our Power." The Rev. Kevin L. Jones of Ebenezer Baptist Church told the NYT that requests from parishioners for help with utility bills now add up to thousands of dollars.Critics have also questioned the SCC's own neutrality. Its chair, Judge Kelsey A. Bagot, was a senior attorney at NextEra less than three years ago. She has declined to recuse herself, arguing that past work with a regulated company has never automatically required a commissioner to step aside.The deal does have backers. Virginia Chamber of Commerce chief Brad N. Hall told the commission the merger would bring more investment into the grid and help build the state's workforce. Still, the SCC staff and the independent monitor for the regional grid have joined the governor and attorney general in opposing it.Even a yes in Richmond would not settle things. The deal also needs clearance from North Carolina, South Carolina and federal regulators. NextEra has tried to buy utilities in Hawaii, North Carolina and Texas before, and each bid fell apart. January will show whether Virginia joins that list.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'Malicious': India flays US court summons to NSA Doval, others over lawsuit by terrorist Pannun
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The ministry of external affairs on Tuesday condemned \"fabricated and malicious\" attacks on New Delhi's officials after the US state department
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The ministry of external affairs on Tuesday condemned "fabricated and malicious" attacks on New Delhi's officials after the US state department reportedly served the government with federal court summons in a civil case filed by designated terrorist Gurupatwant Singh Pannun.During the weekly press briefing, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal termed the lawsuit as "frivolous", saying that requests for the service of judicial documents can only be routed through India's designated central authority."We reject the fabricated and malicious attacks on our high officials, as also the frivolous lawsuits," Jaiswal said."Requests for the service of judicial documents in India can only be routed through India's designated central authority, that is, the ministry of law and justice," he added.Last month, the US state department served federal court summons to New Delhi after Sikh separatist Pannun named number of Indian officials, including national security adviser (NSA) Ajit Doval and former chief of the Research and Analysis Wing (R&AW) Samant Goel.The order marks a fresh procedural development in the lawsuit, which concerns an alleged plot to assassinate Pannun in New York in 2023.The civil lawsuit is linked to the US department of justice's investigation into Nikhil Gupta, an Indian national described as a drug and arms smuggler.Gupta was arrested in the Czech Republic in 2023 before being extradited to the US.US prosecutors accused Gupta of conspiring with others to arrange the assassination of Pannun by hiring a hitman. According to the indictment, Gupta worked with Vikash Yadav, who was allegedly associated with the Research and Analysis Wing (RAW).In response to the allegations, the New Delhi set up a committee to investigate the concerns raised by Washington. Yadav, meanwhile, is facing a case in an Indian court.India has rejected Pannun's civil lawsuit, calling it "unwarranted and unsubstantiated".Get the latest India News and Live updates.
